claim: Mouse ES cell lines were derived from blastula embryos harboring fluorescent reporters that indelibly label cardinal populations of spinal neurons.
source: We isolated four independent ES cell lines containing the V1 reporter En1:Cre/tdTomato, two lines with the V2a reporter Chx10:Cre/tdTomato, seven lines with the V3 reporter Sim1:Cre/tdTomato, and two lines with the motor neuron reporter tgHb9-GFP (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number and types of ES cell lines isolated with specific fluorescent reporters.

claim: ES cells were differentiated into neurospheres containing ~50,000 aggregated cells using retinoic acid (RA) and smoothened agonist (SAG).
source: These ES cell lines were differentiated into neurospheres containing ~50,000 aggregated cells using retinoic acid (RA) and smoothened agonist (SAG) following procedures similar to those described for generating motor neurons (Peljto et al., 2010; Wichterle and Peljto, 2008; Wichterle et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript describes the differentiation protocol with specific cell numbers and reagents, citing previous methods.

claim: ES-cell-derived neurospheres could be maintained for weeks in culture and contained glia and multiple neuronal subtypes.
source: These ES-cell-derived neurospheres could be maintained for weeks in culture and were found to contain glia and multiple neuronal subtypes (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript states the culture duration and cellular composition, with reference to Figure 1B showing immunostaining of cell types.

claim: ES-cell-derived cellular aggregates did not adopt a morphological organization resembling the neural tube or spinal cord.
source: These cellular aggregates did not appear to adopt a morphological organization that resembled the neural tube or spinal cord, rather neurons and glia seemed to be randomly distributed within the spheres (Figure 1B, data not shown).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the lack of organized morphology based on observations.

claim: At 5nM SAG, dorsally located V1 interneurons were enriched compared to ventral V3 interneurons and motor neurons.
source: At 5nM SAG, dorsally located V1 interneurons were enriched compared to ventral V3 interneurons and motor neurons (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The manuscript states the enrichment pattern at specific SAG concentration with reference to quantification figures.

claim: V3 interneurons were preferentially generated at the expense of V1 interneurons in 1000 nM SAG.
source: V3 interneurons were preferentially generated at the expense of V1 interneurons in 1000 nM SAG, whereas motor neurons were most enriched using 50–200 nM SAG (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the differential generation of neuron subtypes at different SAG concentrations.

claim: Motor neurons were most enriched using 50–200 nM SAG.
source: V3 interneurons were preferentially generated at the expense of V1 interneurons in 1000 nM SAG, whereas motor neurons were most enriched using 50–200 nM SAG (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The manuscript specifies the optimal SAG concentration range for motor neuron generation.

claim: Up to 30% of the cells within a neurosphere were V1, V3, or motor neurons using the optimal SAG concentration for each neuronal subtype.
source: In each case, up to 30% of the cells within a neurosphere were V1, V3, or motor neurons using the optimal SAG concentration for each neuronal subtype, with similar results observed for each of the independent stem cell lines.
evidence: The manuscript quantifies the maximum percentage of specific neuron types achieved.

claim: Blocking the notch-delta signaling pathway with DAPT improved V2a interneuron generation.
source: We found, however, that blocking the notch-delta signaling pathway with the gamma secretase inhibitor DAPT improved V2a interneuron generation consistent with previous developmental studies on specification of this interneuron subtype (Del Barrio et al., 2007; Brown et al., 2014; Crone et al., 2008) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results showing improved V2a generation with DAPT treatment, citing previous studies.

claim: RNA-sequencing of FACS purified ES-cell-derived motor neurons and V2a interneurons revealed that each expressed a battery of genes consistent with their identity assignment.
source: In addition to the cardinal marker used to label each cell type (Figure 1A), RNA-sequencing of FACS purified ES-cell-derived motor neurons and V2a interneurons revealed that each expressed a battery of genes consistent with their identity assignment (Al-Mosawie et al., 2007; Brown et al., 2014; Kimura et al., 2006; Kutejova et al., 2016; Lundfald et al., 2007; Saueressig et al., 1999; Wichterle et al., 2002; Xu and Sakiyama-Elbert, 2015; Zhang et al., 2008) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports RNA-seq results confirming cell identity with multiple literature citations.

claim: ES-cell-derived neurons formed numerous excitatory synapses in culture.
source: We observed that ES-cell-derived neurons formed numerous excitatory synapses in culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The manuscript describes immunostaining observations showing synapse formation.

claim: Matured neurospheres produce spontaneous bursts of activity.
source: To investigate whether matured neurospheres likewise produce spontaneous bursts, we monitored network output using both an extracellular suction recording electrode and calcium imaging dyes and found the cell permeable calcium dyes provided an accurate measure of neuronal activity (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of spontaneous bursting using multiple recording methods.

claim: Cell permeable calcium dyes provided an accurate measure of neuronal activity.
source: To investigate whether matured neurospheres likewise produce spontaneous bursts, we monitored network output using both an extracellular suction recording electrode and calcium imaging dyes and found the cell permeable calcium dyes provided an accurate measure of neuronal activity (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: The manuscript validates calcium dye imaging by comparing it to electrical recordings.

claim: Bursting within the spheres was highly synchronized across many neurons.
source: Imaging neuronal activity revealed that bursting within the spheres was highly synchronized across many neurons, suggesting the cells were interconnected (Video 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes calcium imaging observations showing synchronized activity.

claim: Synchronized bursting suggests the cells were interconnected.
source: Imaging neuronal activity revealed that bursting within the spheres was highly synchronized across many neurons, suggesting the cells were interconnected (Video 1).
evidence: The manuscript infers interconnection from the observation of synchronized activity.

claim: CirL spheres produced bursts with lower amplitude and higher frequency than CirH spheres.
source: We found that CirL spheres produced bursts with lower amplitude and higher frequency than CirH spheres (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative comparisons of burst parameters between two conditions.

claim: CirH spheres are enriched in V3 interneurons but are nonetheless heterogenous mixtures of ventral-spinal cord cell types.
source: Since CirH produced reliable high-amplitude bursts, these circuitoids were used to examine the development of and physiological basis for this neuronal activity. CirH spheres are enriched in V3 interneurons but are nonetheless heterogenous mixtures of ventral-spinal cord cell types.
evidence: The manuscript describes the cellular composition of CirH spheres.

claim: Circuitoids were spontaneously active at two weeks and bursting increased in frequency at week 5.
source: We found that these circuitoids were spontaneously active at two weeks and bursting increased in frequency at week 5 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports developmental time course of spontaneous activity.

claim: Acetylcholine receptor antagonists did not significantly alter the spontaneous bursting of circuitoids.
source: Acetylcholine receptor antagonists did not significantly alter the spontaneous bursting of circuitoids (Figure 2B), whereas the glutamatergic AMPA receptor antagonist, CNQX, blocked the activity suggesting that excitatory synaptic drive is necessary for coordinated bursts (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports pharmacological experiments showing no effect of cholinergic antagonists.

claim: The glutamatergic AMPA receptor antagonist, CNQX, blocked circuitoid activity.
source: Acetylcholine receptor antagonists did not significantly alter the spontaneous bursting of circuitoids (Figure 2B), whereas the glutamatergic AMPA receptor antagonist, CNQX, blocked the activity suggesting that excitatory synaptic drive is necessary for coordinated bursts (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports pharmacological experiments showing CNQX blocks activity.

claim: Excitatory synaptic drive is necessary for coordinated bursts in circuitoids.
source: Acetylcholine receptor antagonists did not significantly alter the spontaneous bursting of circuitoids (Figure 2B), whereas the glutamatergic AMPA receptor antagonist, CNQX, blocked the activity suggesting that excitatory synaptic drive is necessary for coordinated bursts (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript infers the necessity of excitatory drive from CNQX blocking experiments.

claim: NMA and 5-HT activate a long-lasting highly regular (rhythmic) pattern of activity from circuitoids that is similar in frequency to fictive locomotor preparations.
source: Remarkably, these drugs activate a long-lasting highly regular (rhythmic) pattern of activity from circuitoids that is similar in frequency to fictive locomotor preparations (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports pharmacological experiments comparing circuitoid activity to known CPG preparations.

claim: Circuitoids acquire network properties that allow the interconnected cells to fire rhythmic bursts.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that circuitoids acquire network properties that allow the interconnected cells to fire rhythmic bursts.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the preceding experimental results.

claim: Most CirH spheres produced regular activity in the evoked condition, but a minority had irregular bursting.
source: We noted, however, that while most CirH spheres produced regular activity in the evoked condition, a minority had irregular bursting (Figure 3A and D).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of variability in circuitoid activity patterns.

claim: When picrotoxin and strychnine were applied, CirH-NR spheres burst in a more regular pattern.
source: When picrotoxin and strychnine, two inhibitory antagonists, were applied, CirH-NR spheres burst in a more regular pattern (Figure 3A–C), suggesting their irregular bursting was caused by the presence of inhibitory neurons.
evidence: The manuscript reports pharmacological experiments showing regularization of bursting.

claim: Irregular bursting in CirH-NR spheres was caused by the presence of inhibitory neurons.
source: When picrotoxin and strychnine, two inhibitory antagonists, were applied, CirH-NR spheres burst in a more regular pattern (Figure 3A–C), suggesting their irregular bursting was caused by the presence of inhibitory neurons.
evidence: The manuscript infers the cause of irregular bursting from the effect of inhibitory antagonists.

claim: CirH-R spheres remained rhythmic in inhibitory antagonists, but their burst frequency slowed.
source: Consistent with this, CirH-R spheres remained rhythmic in inhibitory antagonists; however, we noted that their burst frequency slowed (Figure 3D–F, see below).
evidence: The manuscript reports pharmacological experiments showing frequency changes.

claim: V3DTA circuitoids failed to burst regularly in drugs that evoke rhythmic CPG activity compared to controls.
source: We found that V3DTA circuitoids failed to burst regularly in drugs that evoke rhythmic CPG activity compared to controls, and they produced these irregular bursts at a higher frequency (Figure 3G–J).
evidence: The manuscript reports experiments using genetic ablation of V3 neurons.

claim: V3DTA circuitoids produced irregular bursts at a higher frequency than controls.
source: We found that V3DTA circuitoids failed to burst regularly in drugs that evoke rhythmic CPG activity compared to controls, and they produced these irregular bursts at a higher frequency (Figure 3G–J).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative comparisons of burst frequency in V3 ablation experiments.

claim: By lowering the inhibitory drive in V3DTA circuitoids with inhibitory antagonists the networks switched to a slower and more regular activity pattern.
source: Interestingly, by lowering the inhibitory drive in V3DTA circuitoids with inhibitory antagonists the networks switched to a slower and more regular activity pattern (Figure 3K–N).
evidence: The manuscript reports pharmacological rescue experiments in V3 ablation circuitoids.

claim: The cellular composition within heterogeneous circuitoids influences the network's activity.
source: These findings reveal that the cellular composition within heterogeneous circuitoids influences the network's activity.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the preceding experiments on cellular composition.

claim: Synthetic networks comprised of only V3 neurons produced large spontaneous bursts of activity.
source: Similar to heterogeneous circuitoids, large spontaneous bursts of activity were observed in synthetic networks comprised of only V3 neurons (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of activity in purified V3 neuron networks.

claim: NMA and 5-HT evoked a rhythmic pattern of activity in V3 networks with a frequency higher than the spontaneous burst rate.
source: Likewise, NMA and 5-HT evoked a rhythmic pattern of activity with a frequency higher than the spontaneous burst rate (Figure 4B, C, S, T).
evidence: The manuscript reports pharmacological experiments on purified V3 networks.

claim: Inhibitory antagonists did not significantly perturb the evoked pattern of bursting in V3 networks.
source: Consistent with the glutamatergic properties of V3 interneurons, inhibitory antagonists did not significantly perturb the evoked pattern of bursting, whereas the glutamatergic antagonist, CNQX, blocked activity (Figure 4C–E and R–T).
evidence: The manuscript reports pharmacological experiments confirming glutamatergic nature of V3 networks.

claim: The glutamatergic antagonist, CNQX, blocked activity in V3 networks.
source: Consistent with the glutamatergic properties of V3 interneurons, inhibitory antagonists did not significantly perturb the evoked pattern of bursting, whereas the glutamatergic antagonist, CNQX, blocked activity (Figure 4C–E and R–T).
evidence: The manuscript reports pharmacological experiments showing CNQX blocks V3 network activity.

claim: Gap junctions appear to be insufficient to sustain rhythmic network activity in the presence of AMPA receptor blockers.
source: If gap junctions are present between cells, they appear to be insufficient to sustain rhythmic network activity in the presence of AMPA receptor blockers.
evidence: The manuscript infers the insufficiency of gap junctions from CNQX blocking experiments.

claim: V3 circuitoid bursting frequency increases as they mature from 17 to 45 days after the initiation of ES cell differentiation.
source: As V3 circuitoids mature from 17 to 45 days after the initiation of ES cell differentiation, we determined that their bursting frequency increases (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports developmental time course of V3 circuitoid activity.

claim: Circuitoids ranging in size from 5000 to 100,000 cells exhibited similar bursting parameters.
source: We also found that circuitoids ranging in size from 5000 to 100,000 cells exhibited similar bursting parameters, suggesting they form highly scalable networks (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experiments testing the effect of network size on activity.

claim: Circuitoids form highly scalable networks.
source: We also found that circuitoids ranging in size from 5000 to 100,000 cells exhibited similar bursting parameters, suggesting they form highly scalable networks (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript infers scalability from the observation that different sized networks have similar properties.

claim: Synthetic networks comprised of synaptically coupled, purified V3 interneurons are sufficient to produce rhythmic bursting in response to drugs that evoke CPG activity.
source: All together, these findings indicate that synthetic networks comprised of synaptically coupled, purified V3 interneurons are sufficient to produce rhythmic bursting in response to drugs that evoke CPG activity.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the preceding experiments on purified V3 networks.

claim: V2a networks displayed spontaneous bursting and became rhythmic in the evoked condition.
source: We purified V2a interneurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,D) and created synthetic networks that were spontaneously active and became rhythmic in the evoked condition (Figure 4F, G and S).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of activity in purified V2a neuron networks.

claim: The amplitude, rhythmicity, and frequency of V2a and V3 networks were similar.
source: The amplitude, rhythmicity, and frequency of V2a and V3 networks were similar (Figure 4R–T).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative comparisons between V2a and V3 network properties.

claim: The burst patterns of V2a excitatory networks were not affected by glycine/GABA antagonists but were disrupted by AMPA receptor blockers.
source: As expected, the burst patterns of V2a excitatory networks were not affected by glycine/GABA antagonists but were disrupted by AMPA receptor blockers (Figure 4G–I and R–T).
evidence: The manuscript reports pharmacological experiments confirming glutamatergic nature of V2a networks.

claim: Networks comprised of purified motor neurons displayed spontaneous bursting and responded to drugs that evoke CPG activity.
source: Networks comprised of purified motor neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), which have recurrent collaterals that synapse onto neighboring motor neurons and interneurons (Eccles et al., 1954; Nishimaru et al., 2005; Renshaw, 1946), also displayed spontaneous bursting and responded to drugs that evoke CPG activity (Figure 4J and K).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of activity in purified motor neuron networks with citations.

claim: Motor neuron network bursts were more irregular and had greater variability between experiments than those produced by V2a and V3 interneuron networks.
source: However, the bursts were more irregular and in general had greater variability between experiments than those produced by the V2a and V3 interneurons networks (Figure 4S).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative observations of motor neuron network properties.

claim: The activity in motor neuron circuitoids was dependent upon glutamatergic signaling rather than acetylcholine.
source: The activity in motor neuron circuitoids was dependent upon glutamatergic signaling rather than acetylcholine (Figure 4K–M and T, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports pharmacological experiments on motor neuron networks.

claim: Motor neuron findings are consistent with the intrinsic burst properties of motor neurons.
source: These findings are consistent with the intrinsic burst properties of motor neurons (Hochman et al., 1994; Kiehn et al., 2000; MacLean et al., 1997), their responsiveness to glutamatergic input (Jahr and Yoshioka, 1986; Rekling et al., 2000), and their co-release of cholinergic and glutamatergic neurotransmitters (Herzog et al., 2004; Lamotte d'Incamps and Ascher, 2008; Meister et al., 1993; Mentis et al., 2005; Nishimaru et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript relates findings to established literature on motor neuron properties.

claim: V1 networks displayed spontaneous activity with burst amplitudes significantly lower than excitatory networks.
source: While spontaneous activity can be observed in V1 networks, the burst amplitudes are significantly lower than excitatory networks and fail to burst rhythmically in drugs that evoke CPG activity (Figure 4N, O, R and S).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of activity in purified V1 neuron networks.

claim: V1 networks fail to burst rhythmically in drugs that evoke CPG activity.
source: While spontaneous activity can be observed in V1 networks, the burst amplitudes are significantly lower than excitatory networks and fail to burst rhythmically in drugs that evoke CPG activity (Figure 4N, O, R and S).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of V1 network response to CPG-evoking drugs.

claim: The low levels of activity found in V1 networks could be due to contamination with small amounts of excitatory neurons.
source: Although cell purifications are >98% pure (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), the low levels of activity found in V1 networks could be due to contamination with small amounts of excitatory neurons because inhibitory antagonists increased burst amplitude and rhythmicity, and a glutamatergic AMPA receptor blocker, CNQX, stopped the activity (Figure 4N–Q and T).
evidence: The manuscript infers possible contamination from pharmacological experiments despite high purity.

claim: Multiple subclasses of excitatory interneurons are sufficient to form rhythmically active networks.
source: These findings reveal a marked difference between the rhythmic activity of excitatory versus inhibitory neuron networks, and indicate that multiple subclasses of excitatory interneurons are sufficient to form rhythmically active networks.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the preceding experiments on different neuron subtypes.

claim: Excitatory V3 interneurons produced a reliable pattern of spontaneous bursts that continually increased in frequency when co-cultured with increasing numbers of inhibitory V1 interneurons.
source: We found that excitatory V3 interneurons produced a reliable pattern of spontaneous bursts that continually increased in frequency when co-cultured with increasing numbers of inhibitory V1 interneurons (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: The manuscript reports experiments on mixed V3-V1 networks with varying E/I ratios.

claim: After application of inhibitory antagonists, V3-V1 co-cultures returned to the bursting pattern observed without V1 neurons.
source: After application of the inhibitory antagonists, the cultures returned to the bursting pattern observed without V1 neurons (Figure 5B, D, F and G).
evidence: The manuscript reports pharmacological experiments showing reversibility of V1 effects.

claim: The effect of inhibitory neurons is mediated by direct synaptic activity rather than causing changes in the development, survival, or physiological properties of V3 cells.
source: First, the effect of inhibitory neurons is mediated by direct synaptic activity rather than causing changes in the development, survival, or physiological properties of V3 cells because picrotoxin and strychnine quickly restored V3 activity to its normal frequency.
evidence: The manuscript infers the mechanism of V1 effects from the rapid reversibility with antagonists.

claim: The addition of V1 cells to V3 networks unlikely changes V3-activity by displacing cells or altering the connectome of the excitatory network.
source: Second, the addition of V1 cells to V3 networks unlikely changes V3-activity by displacing cells or altering the connectome of the excitatory network because drug inhibitors of V1 interneurons restore normal V3-activity.
evidence: The manuscript infers that V1 cells don't alter network structure from the reversibility of their effects.

claim: Excitatory networks may tune their burst rate by flexibly recruiting different numbers of inhibitory neurons.
source: Third, excitatory networks may tune their burst rate by flexibly recruiting different numbers of inhibitory neurons.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanism based on the preceding experimental results.

claim: V1 interneurons had little influence on the burst frequency of motor neurons, but instead caused greater burst amplitude variation.
source: Unlike V3 networks, V1 interneurons had little influence on the burst frequency of motor neurons, but instead caused greater burst amplitude variation (Figure 5C and E–G).
evidence: The manuscript reports experiments on mixed motor neuron-V1 networks showing different effects than V3-V1 networks.

claim: In networks with a 10:1 motor neuron/V1 ratio, separate regions of interest could burst independently.
source: In networks with a 10:1 motor neuron/V1 ratio, we found that separate regions of interest (ROI) could burst independently (Figure 6A, Video 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of segmented activity in motor neuron-V1 networks.

claim: Changes in the coordination of neuronal activity across the network were not due to depletion of excitatory interconnections among motor neurons or a physical alteration of the circuit's connectome.
source: Changes in the coordination of neuronal activity across the network were not due to depletion of excitatory interconnections among motor neurons or a physical alteration of the circuit's connectome, because inhibitory antagonists caused the network to rapidly switch back into a synchronous bursting pattern (Figure 6B, Video 3).
evidence: The manuscript infers that network structure is unchanged from the rapid reversibility with antagonists.

claim: Inhibitory V1 interneurons lacked the ability to create complexity within V3 networks.
source: Interestingly, inhibitory V1 interneurons lacked the ability to create complexity within V3 networks (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis showing no complexity increase in V3-V1 networks.

claim: Within tripartite circuitoids motor neurons displayed the same coordinated pattern of activity as the interneurons and fired synchronously as a single unit.
source: We found that within tripartite circuitoids motor neurons displayed the same coordinated pattern of activity as the interneurons and fired synchronously as a single unit within the culture across a range of V1 cell numbers (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of motor neuron activity in tripartite networks.

claim: V3 interneurons displayed higher frequencies of miniature events than motor neurons in a pure motor neuron network.
source: Within V3 networks, V3 interneurons displayed higher frequencies of miniature events than motor neurons in a pure motor neuron network (Figure 7H,I,K).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological recordings comparing mEPSC frequencies.

claim: Identified motor neurons in mixed V3-motor neuron circuitoids had similar mEPSC frequencies as the V3 interneurons in V3 networks.
source: Interestingly, the identified motor neurons in mixed V3-motor neuron circuitoids had similar mEPSC frequencies as the V3 interneurons in V3 networks (Figure 7H–K).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological recordings comparing mEPSC frequencies in mixed networks.

claim: The V3 cell-type may strongly bind the activity of neurons within a network due to a greater probability of neurotransmitter release or by providing an increased number of synaptic release sites.
source: This analysis indicates that the V3 cell-type may strongly bind the activity of neurons within a network due to a greater probability of neurotransmitter release or by providing an increased number of synaptic release sites.
evidence: The manuscript infers possible mechanisms from the mEPSC frequency data.

claim: Inhibitory neurons act in a context-dependent manner to regulate the frequency of bursting and the pattern (i.e. segmentation) of the network activity.
source: We found that inhibitory neurons act in a context-dependent manner to regulate the frequency of bursting and the pattern (i.e. segmentation) of the network activity.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main findings from the experiments on E/I ratios.

claim: Interconnected excitatory and inhibitory neurons can transition to different output based on cell-type-specific connection-strength hierarchies working in combination with controls that gate the relative activity-ratio of E-to-I cells.
source: Our findings lead to a model whereby interconnected excitatory and inhibitory neurons can transition to different output based on cell-type-specific connection-strength hierarchies working in combination with controls that gate the relative activity-ratio of E-to-I cells (Figure 8).
evidence: The manuscript proposes a model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Rhythmic neuronal activity that is coordinated across circuits comprised of interconnected neurons is a general property found in many areas of the CNS.
source: Rhythmic neuronal activity that is coordinated across circuits comprised of interconnected neurons is a general property found in many areas of the CNS (Buzsaki, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about rhythmic activity in the CNS.

claim: Rhythmic activity probably arises when irregular spikes randomly produced by interconnected excitatory neurons become integrated across dendritic trees, thereby converging into a regular oscillatory pattern of output shared by cells across the network.
source: This activity pattern probably arises when irregular spikes randomly produced by interconnected excitatory neurons become integrated across dendritic trees, thereby converging into a regular oscillatory pattern of output shared by cells across the network (Softky and Koch, 1993).
evidence: The manuscript cites a theoretical explanation for rhythmic activity.

claim: Inhibitory neurons are considered important components of dynamic neural networks, because they can impose a regulated pattern on the system.
source: Thus, inhibitory (I) cells are considered important components of dynamic neural networks, because they can impose a regulated pattern on the system (Brown, 1911; Buzsaki, 2006; Goulding et al., 2014; Grillner and Jessell, 2009; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Marder and Bucher, 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about the role of inhibitory neurons.

claim: Ablation of inhibitory V1 neurons slows the burst frequency of the CPG.
source: Ablation of inhibitory V1 neurons slows the burst frequency of the CPG (Gosgnach et al., 2006), whereas ablation of both V1 and V2b inhibitory neurons disrupts the coordination of flexor-extensor alternation (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on V1 neuron ablation effects.

claim: Ablation of both V1 and V2b inhibitory neurons disrupts the coordination of flexor-extensor alternation.
source: Ablation of inhibitory V1 neurons slows the burst frequency of the CPG (Gosgnach et al., 2006), whereas ablation of both V1 and V2b inhibitory neurons disrupts the coordination of flexor-extensor alternation (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on V1 and V2b neuron ablation effects.

claim: Removing the V2a or V3 excitatory neurons from the network results in more irregular CPG bursting.
source: Removing the V2a or V3 excitatory neurons from the network results in more irregular CPG bursting (Crone et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on V2a and V3 neuron ablation effects.

claim: The oscillatory networks studied in this report lacked the structured inhibition that underlies left-right and flexor-extensor coordination found in complex CPG networks such as the lumbar spinal cord.
source: The oscillatory networks studied in this report lacked the structured inhibition that underlies left-right and flexor-extensor coordination found in complex CPG networks such as the lumbar spinal cord (Kullander et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges limitations of the circuitoid model compared to in vivo CPGs.

claim: The oscillatory activity of circuitoid networks was more akin to a half-center CPG or respiratory CPG, which produce regular on-off bursts.
source: Rather, the oscillatory activity of circuitoid networks was more akin to a half-center CPG or respiratory CPG, which produce regular on-off bursts (Garcia-Campmany et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript compares circuitoid activity to simpler CPG types with citation.

claim: Circuitoid oscillations were synaptically driven by glutamate, like CPGs.
source: (1) Circuitoid oscillations were synaptically driven by glutamate, like CPGs (Beato et al., 1997; Hägglund et al., 2010; Kiehn et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript compares circuitoid properties to CPGs with citations.

claim: Circuitoids displayed spontaneous activity that resembled the spontaneous bursts recorded from isolated spinal cords.
source: (2) Circuitoids displayed spontaneous activity that resembled the spontaneous bursts recorded from isolated spinal cords (Myers et al., 2005; O'Donovan and Landmesser, 1987; Whelan et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript compares circuitoid properties to CPGs with citations.

claim: Circuitoids became rhythmically active in drugs that evoke CPG activity.
source: (3) Circuitoids became rhythmically active in drugs that evoke CPG activity (Jiang et al., 1999; Kudo and Yamada, 1987; Smith and Feldman, 1987; Whelan et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript compares circuitoid properties to CPGs with citations.

claim: The frequency of bursts produced by circuitoids was in a similar range to those produced by the spinal CPG.
source: (4) The frequency of bursts produced by circuitoids was in a similar range to those produced by the spinal CPG (Talpalar and Kiehn, 2010; Whelan et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript compares circuitoid properties to CPGs with citations.

claim: The ablation of V3 interneurons from circuitoids degraded the rhythmicity analogous to the phenotype caused by ablating V3 cells in vivo.
source: (5) The ablation of V3 interneurons from circuitoids degraded the rhythmicity analogous to the phenotype caused by ablating V3 cells in vivo (Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript compares circuitoid properties to CPGs with citations.

claim: Like spinal CPGs, circuitoid rhythms could occur in the absence of inhibition.
source: (6) Like spinal CPGs, circuitoid rhythms could occur in the absence of inhibition (Bracci et al., 1996; Cowley and Schmidt, 1995; Kremer and Lev-Tov, 1997).
evidence: The manuscript compares circuitoid properties to CPGs with citations.

claim: In both circuitoids and CPGs blocking inhibitory V1 interneuron function reduced the burst speed.
source: (7) In both circuitoids and CPGs blocking inhibitory V1 interneuron function reduced the burst speed (Cowley and Schmidt, 1995; Gosgnach et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript compares circuitoid properties to CPGs with citations.

claim: Flexibility within rhythmic circuits can be achieved by constructing networks with neurons that have unequal synaptic interactions, and by regulating the activity-ratio of excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: Our observations suggest that flexibility within rhythmic circuits can be achieved by constructing networks with neurons that have unequal synaptic interactions, and by regulating the activity-ratio of excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Unequal synaptic interactions and activity-ratio regulation are sufficient to control the speed and segmentation of bursting.
source: Together these features are sufficient to control the speed and segmentation of bursting.
evidence: The manuscript concludes about sufficiency based on the experimental results.

claim: Circuitoids could be used to study neurological diseases that affect circuits.
source: It has not escaped our notice that circuitoids could be used to study neurological diseases that affect circuits and might represent transplantable modules for nervous system repair.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about potential applications of circuitoids.

claim: Circuitoids might represent transplantable modules for nervous system repair.
source: It has not escaped our notice that circuitoids could be used to study neurological diseases that affect circuits and might represent transplantable modules for nervous system repair.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about potential applications of circuitoids.
